newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Mass murderer "accepts" he should rot in jail.
newsitem.headline: Mass murderer "accepts" he should rot in jail.

text.p: Martin Bryant accepts that he should languish and die in jail for the mass murder of 35 persons at Port Arthur last April but will not divulge his motive, the lawyer for the confessed killer told a court on Wednesday.

Addressing the sentencing hearing in the Tasmanian Supreme Court, the lawyer painted the 29-year-old Bryant, who methodically shot his victims, as a lonely man of impaired intelligence who knew right from wrong and was not criminally insane.

"Martin Bryant accepts that in all probability he will never be released from prison and will die there and he also accepts that that would be a not inappropriate sentence," defence lawyer John Avery told an emotion-charged courtroom.
Bryant who has seemed relaxed and amused by the proceedings, blushed in the dock as details of his severely limited intelligence were read out at the end of the two-day hearing.
He will appear in court once more on Friday for sentence.
Bryant appears to suffer a rare, untreatable disorder called Asperger's Syndrome, which affects about three percent of the population and is similar to autism, the court heard.
But unlike others with this condition, he craves attention and has appeared at times to almost revel in his notoriety, the court was told.

"There is no such (insanity) defence available to him," Prosecutor Damian Bugg told the court, which was packed with distraught family of the 35 victims and massacre survivors. "He is criminally responsible for his acts," he added.

On April 28, a crisp autumn afternoon, Bryant opened fire among the ruins of the old penal colony at Port Arthur in this southern island state in a crime that so shocked the nation it has since been likened to a natural disaster.
Defence lawyer Avery agreed on Wednesday the killings could be termed a slaughter but offered no motive.
"I am instructed to make no submissions or place before the court any explanation or reason for this massacre, other than can be gleaned from the medical material," he said.
"The reason, the answer for the burning question 'why?' must for the time being remain with the accused."

The court heard that Bryant, a childhood bully who liked to torment animals, had been virtually friendless all his life and was nursing a deep, angry grudge against the world in the 12 months before he opened fire at the Port Arthur historic site.
His only real companion, an eccentric middle-aged woman who paid him to run errands, had died in 1992 and his father, his only other controlling influence, committed suicide the following year.
Bryant's grudges went back to his childhood in the Port Arthur area, where he spent holidays and where he felt he had at times been humiliated by historic site staff, the court heard.
He also disliked the owners of a guesthouse there, David and Noelene Martin, who were his first victims on April 28.

"These trivial events, in combination with the long-standing resentment of Mr and Mrs Martin, may have been enough to give the specific direction to Bryant's explosion of resentment against the world," Avery quoted a medical report as saying.
Bryant initially denied all the charges, telling police he went surfing that day, but two weeks ago week he reversed his pleas, laughing and smirking as he did so.
Psychiatrist Ian Sale, who interviewed Bryant in jail on behalf of the prosecution, said Bryant was neither mad nor bad.
"I think he's basically wired up badly," Sale said in a television interview aired after the hearing on Wednesday.
